Photometric observations of the star KOI-3278 made with the Kepler space telescope showed that its brightness periodically increases slightly (see the figures). This effect can be explained by the phenomenon of gravitational microlensing. An invisible object (the lens) orbits the star. When it is between the star (the source) and the observer, its gravity focuses and amplifies the light of the source. The maximum amplification is
$$A = 1 + 2\left(\frac{R_E}{R}\right)^2, \qquad\text{where:}\qquad R_E = \sqrt{\frac{4GM}{c^2}D_L\left(1 - \frac{D_L}{D_S}\right)};$$
$R$ is the radius of the star, $R_E$ – the so-called Einstein radius, $M$ – the mass of the lens, and $D_L$ and $D_S$ are respectively the distances of the lens and of the source from the observer.

Using the available data and knowing that the source is a main-sequence star of mass $1.04\,M_\odot$ and radius $0.96\,R_\odot$, calculate the mass of the lensing object.

By analogy we can also speak of the phenomenon of a mini minimoon.

5) The James Webb Space Telescope

On 25 December 2021 the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) was launched into space. After reaching the vicinity of the second Lagrange point $L_2$, the telescope is to observe distant parts of the cosmos in the infrared, so the instruments on board must be kept at a suitably low temperature ($\leqslant 40$ K).

Unfortunately, the telescope is heated all the time by two heat sources: the sunlight falling on the telescope and the electronics on board (the heating by light from the observed objects is non-zero, but negligible in comparison).

To cope with this, a sunshield of metallised foil in the shape of a kite with diagonals of 14.2 m and 21.2 m was designed. The shield has five layers, each of which reflects 90% of the radiation reaching it. The gaps between the layers allow the heat accumulated in the shield material to be carried away sideways.

The mirror and the detectors are placed in the shadow of the shield on the side opposite the Sun (the so-called "cold side"). The other systems of the telescope and the radiators carrying away heat are on the sunward side of the shield (the so-called "warm side"). In total the radiators carry away about 2 kW of thermal energy.

a) Calculate the mean temperature of the outer layer of the shield on the "warm side", taking into account the influence of the Sun and of the energy coming from the telescope systems. Show that the energy coming from the telescope has little influence on the mean temperature. Neglect the influence of the further layers.

The Lagrange point $L_2$ is located $1.492\times10^9$ m from the Earth in the direction opposite to the Sun. You may assume that the shield material reflects all wavelengths uniformly and that the shield is perpendicular to the light falling from the Sun.

Note: the high temperatures of the "warm side" quoted in the media are maximum values that some places on the telescope may reach, not the mean value.

b) Correct the mean temperature of the outer layer of the shield on the "warm side", taking into account the influence of the neighbouring layer. Assume that the layers are parallel.

c) Estimate the mean temperature of the last layer on the "cold side", assuming that energy reaches the "cold side" only through the shield. Describe the other assumptions made.

The Hubble parameter describes the rate of expansion of the Universe and is defined as:

$$H(t) = \frac{1}{a(t)}\,\frac{\Delta a(t)}{\Delta t}$$

where $a(t)$ is the scale factor, and $\Delta a(t)$ is the change of the scale factor in a small time interval $\Delta t$.
